stem: What kind of mixture is separated by fractional distillation?

options.content: Liquids that mix completely and have different boiling points
options.rationale: For example ethanol and water.

options.content: An insoluble solid and a liquid
options.rationale: That mixture is separated by filtration.

options.content: A dissolved solid and its solvent
options.rationale: Simple distillation or evaporation is used for that.

options.content: Several coloured dyes dissolved in a little water
options.rationale: Chromatography separates small amounts of dyes.

explanation: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids (liquids that mix completely) that have different boiling points, such as ethanol and water, or the hydrocarbons in crude oil.

stem: A mixture of ethanol (boiling point $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and water (boiling point $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$) is fractionally distilled. Which liquid is collected first, and why?

options.content: Ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point
options.rationale: The more volatile liquid reaches the top of the column first.

options.content: Water, because it has the higher boiling point
options.rationale: The liquid with the higher boiling point condenses in the column and runs back.

options.content: Water, because there is more of it in the mixture
options.rationale: The order depends on boiling point, not on the amount.

options.content: Both distil together, so neither comes first
options.rationale: The fractionating column separates them, so ethanol comes over first.

explanation: Ethanol boils at a lower temperature than water, so its vapour reaches the top of the fractionating column first and is collected at about 78 °C. Water condenses in the column and runs back until the ethanol has gone.

stem: True or false: in fractional distillation, the thermometer bulb should be placed in the boiling liquid.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite: the bulb goes level with the side arm at the top of the column, where it measures the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: the bulb is level with the side arm, so it shows the boiling point of the vapour being collected.

explanation: The thermometer bulb is placed level with the side arm at the top of the column. It measures the temperature of the vapour passing into the condenser, which tells you which liquid is distilling.

stem: What is the purpose of the glass beads packed into a fractionating column?

options.content: They give a large surface area on which vapour repeatedly condenses and evaporates.
options.rationale: Each cycle enriches the vapour in the lower-boiling liquid.

options.content: They filter out the liquid with the higher boiling point.
options.rationale: Nothing is filtered: the separation depends on boiling points.

options.content: They react with water vapour and remove it.
options.rationale: Glass beads are unreactive.

options.content: They stop the mixture boiling too quickly, like anti-bumping granules.
options.rationale: Anti-bumping granules go in the flask; the beads are in the column.

explanation: The beads provide a large surface area. Vapour condenses on them and is re-evaporated by hot vapour from below many times; each time it becomes richer in the lower-boiling liquid, so a good separation is achieved.

stem: A mixture of propanone (boiling point $56\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and water is fractionally distilled. What does the thermometer read while the first fraction is being collected?

options.content: About $56\ ^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: The first fraction is propanone, the liquid with the lower boiling point.

options.content: About $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: Water distils later, once the propanone has gone.

options.content: About $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: That is the average of the two boiling points, which has no meaning here.

options.content: About $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$
options.rationale: Room temperature: nothing distils until the vapour reaches its boiling point.

explanation: The thermometer at the side arm shows the boiling point of the liquid distilling. Propanone, with the lower boiling point, distils first, at about 56 °C.
hints: Which liquid has the lower boiling point?

stem: $80.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of a mixture of propanone and water is fractionally distilled. $30.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of distillate is collected at $56\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Assume that this fraction is pure propanone and that all the propanone was collected. Calculate the percentage by volume of propanone in the mixture.
explanation: Percentage of propanone $= \dfrac{30.0}{80.0} \times 100 = 37.5\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Volume of propanone $= 30.0\ \text{cm}^3$ (the fraction collected at $56\ ^\circ\text{C}$).
2. Percentage $= \dfrac{30.0}{80.0} \times 100 = 37.5\%$.
hints: The fraction collected at the boiling point of propanone is the propanone.

stem: A mixture of pentane (boiling point $36\ ^\circ\text{C}$), heptane ($98\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and hexane ($69\ ^\circ\text{C}$) is fractionally distilled. Match each liquid with when it is collected. One description is not used.

right.content: Never distils: it stays in the flask

explanation: The liquids distil in order of boiling point, lowest first: pentane (36 °C), then hexane (69 °C), then heptane (98 °C). All three boil well below the temperatures reached, so all of them distil.
hints: Put the boiling points in order, lowest first.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Fractional distillation separates liquids that are {{blank:mix}} and have different {{blank:property}}.

explanation: Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids (which mix completely) by their different boiling points. Immiscible liquids, which form layers, are separated with a separating funnel.

stem: Name the piece of apparatus, packed with glass beads, that is fitted between the flask and the condenser in fractional distillation.

rejected.feedback: The condenser cools the vapour. The tube packed with glass beads is the fractionating column.
The tube packed with glass beads is the fractionating column.

explanation: The fractionating column is a vertical tube packed with glass beads or rings. It separates the vapours by repeated condensation and evaporation.

stem: A mixture of ethanol and water is to be fractionally distilled. Why is an electric heater safer than a Bunsen burner for heating it?

options.content: A Bunsen burner cannot reach 100 °C.
options.rationale: A Bunsen flame is far hotter than 100 °C.

options.content: Ethanol is flammable, and its vapour could catch fire in a naked flame.
options.rationale: Avoiding naked flames removes the ignition source.

options.content: Electric heaters make the beads in the column work better.
options.rationale: The heat source does not affect the beads.

options.content: Water reacts with the gas from a Bunsen burner.
options.rationale: There is no such reaction.

explanation: Ethanol is highly flammable. If any vapour escapes, a naked flame could ignite it, so an electric heater (or heating mantle) is used.
hints: Think about the hazards of ethanol.

stem: Why is simple distillation not suitable for separating ethanol from water?

options.content: Ethanol and water are immiscible, so they form two layers.
options.rationale: They mix completely: they are miscible.

options.content: Ethanol decomposes before it reaches its boiling point.
options.rationale: Ethanol boils at 78 °C without decomposing.

options.content: Water does not evaporate at all during simple distillation.
options.rationale: Water evaporates well below its boiling point and boils at 100 °C.

options.content: Their close boiling points let water distil over with the ethanol.
options.rationale: A fractionating column is needed to separate liquids with close boiling points.

explanation: Simple distillation works when the boiling points are very different, as with water and salt. Ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C) are close enough that both evaporate together, so a fractionating column is needed for a good separation.
hints: Compare the boiling points: how far apart are they?

stem: Liquid air contains nitrogen (boiling point $-196\ ^\circ\text{C}$), argon ($-186\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and oxygen ($-183\ ^\circ\text{C}$). It is allowed to warm up slowly in a fractionating column. Which gas boils off first?

options.content: Oxygen
options.rationale: Oxygen has the highest boiling point of the three, so it boils off last.

options.content: Argon
options.rationale: Argon boils between nitrogen and oxygen.

options.content: Nitrogen
options.rationale: It has the lowest boiling point (−196 °C).

options.content: All three boil off together
options.rationale: Their different boiling points let them be separated.

explanation: The lowest boiling point is the most negative: nitrogen at −196 °C. As the liquid air warms, nitrogen boils off first, then argon, then oxygen.

stem: Where is the temperature highest in a fractionating column during distillation?

options.content: At the top
options.rationale: The top is the coolest part; only the most volatile vapour gets there.

options.content: At the bottom
options.rationale: The column is hottest just above the boiling mixture and cools towards the top.

options.content: In the middle
options.rationale: The temperature falls steadily from bottom to top.

options.content: It is the same everywhere
options.rationale: There is a temperature gradient, which is what makes the separation work.

explanation: The column is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. Liquids with higher boiling points condense lower down; the most volatile liquid reaches the top.
hints: Where is the source of heat?

stem:
Tatenda fractionally distils a mixture of ethanol and water and records the thermometer reading after each $5\ \text{cm}^3$ of distillate.

| Volume of distillate / cm³ | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | 35 | 40 | 45 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature / °C | 78 | 78 | 78 | 78 | 81 | 94 | 100 | 100 | 100 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State the boiling point of the liquid collected in the first fraction.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the liquid collected in the first fraction.

rejected.feedback: Water boils at 100 °C. The first fraction, at 78 °C, is ethanol.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why does the temperature rise between 20 cm³ and 35 cm³?

options.content: The heater has been turned up halfway through the run.
options.rationale: The rise is caused by the change in what is distilling.

options.content: The ethanol has started to decompose in the hot flask.
options.rationale: Ethanol does not decompose at these temperatures.

options.content: Nearly all the ethanol has distilled, so the vapour becomes water.
options.rationale: The temperature rises to the boiling point of water.

options.content: The condenser has stopped cooling the vapour properly.
options.rationale: The condenser does not affect the thermometer reading at the side arm.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe how Tatenda should collect the ethanol and the water as separate fractions.

points.description: Collect the distillate in one receiver while the temperature stays at 78 °C
Change the receiver when the temperature starts to rise (above 78 °C) and collect the water separately at 100 °C

parts.explanation: Collect the distillate in one receiver while the thermometer stays at 78 °C: this is the ethanol fraction. As soon as the temperature starts to rise, change the receiver; collect the fraction that distils at 100 °C (water) in a fresh receiver.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Why is the thermometer bulb placed level with the side arm?

options.content: To measure the temperature of the boiling mixture
options.rationale: The bulb would have to be in the liquid for that.

options.content: To stop the vapour escaping through the side arm
options.rationale: The thermometer does not seal anything.

options.content: To cool the vapour before it reaches the condenser
options.rationale: The condenser cools the vapour.

options.content: To measure the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser
options.rationale: This is the boiling point of the liquid being collected.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: State **one** safety precaution for this experiment.

points.description: Any one: heat with an electric heater / water bath, not a naked flame (ethanol is flammable); wear eye protection; use anti-bumping granules; do not heat a closed system

parts.explanation: Ethanol is flammable, so heat the flask with an electric heater rather than a naked flame (and wear eye protection).

explanation: The first fraction distils at 78 °C, the boiling point of ethanol. When almost all the ethanol has distilled, the temperature rises to 100 °C as water distils. Changing the receiver when the temperature rises keeps the fractions separate. The thermometer at the side arm reads the temperature of the vapour entering the condenser. Ethanol is flammable, so naked flames are avoided.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** 78 °C.
2. **(b)** Ethanol.
3. **(c)** The ethanol has nearly all distilled; water vapour (100 °C) now reaches the thermometer.
4. **(d)** Collect at 78 °C; change the receiver when the temperature rises; collect water at 100 °C.
5. **(e)** It measures the vapour entering the condenser.
6. **(f)** No naked flame (ethanol is flammable) / eye protection.
hints: Each flat part of the temperature record is one liquid distilling.

stem: A community group extracts eucalyptus oil from leaves by **steam distillation**. Steam from a boiling flask is passed through crushed eucalyptus leaves in a second flask. The vapour that leaves is cooled in a condenser, and the distillate collected in a beaker forms two layers. The oil layer is on top.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is steam distillation used instead of heating the leaves until the oil boils?

options.content: The oil has a much lower boiling point than water does.
options.rationale: The oil has a much higher boiling point than water.

options.content: Steam carries the oil over below 100 °C, before it can decompose.
options.rationale: Steam distillation protects heat-sensitive oils.

options.content: Steam reacts with the oil to make it more fragrant.
options.rationale: Steam carries the oil; it does not react with it.

options.content: Steam dissolves the leaves and releases the oil.
options.rationale: The leaves stay behind in the flask.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why does the distillate form two layers?

options.content: The oil has reacted with the water.
options.rationale: No reaction takes place.

options.content: The water has frozen.
options.rationale: The distillate is a liquid at room temperature.

options.content: Oil and water are immiscible: they do not mix.
options.rationale: Immiscible liquids form separate layers.

options.content: The oil is a solid.
options.rationale: The oil is a liquid that floats on water.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the piece of apparatus used to separate the two layers.

rejected.feedback: A filter funnel separates a solid from a liquid. Two liquid layers are separated with a separating funnel.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The oil layer floats on top of the water. What does this show?

options.content: The oil is denser than water.
options.rationale: A denser liquid would sink to the bottom.

options.content: The oil has a lower boiling point than water.
options.rationale: Which layer is on top depends on density, not boiling point.

options.content: The oil dissolves in water.
options.rationale: If it dissolved, there would be only one layer.

options.content: The oil is less dense than water.
options.rationale: The less dense liquid forms the upper layer.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Give **two** uses of plant oils obtained by steam distillation.

points.description: Any one different: flavourings / medicines (for example cough remedies) / insect repellents / aromatherapy

parts.explanation: Steam-distilled oils are used in perfumes and soaps, as flavourings, in medicines such as eucalyptus cough remedies and as insect repellents.

explanation: Essential oils boil at high temperatures and would decompose, but steam carries them over below 100 °C. Oil and water are immiscible, so the distillate separates into two layers; the less dense oil floats on top and is separated with a separating funnel. The oils are used in perfumes, flavourings, medicines and insect repellents.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** The oil would decompose at its boiling point; steam distils it below 100 °C.
2. **(b)** Oil and water are immiscible.
3. **(c)** A separating funnel.
4. **(d)** The oil is less dense than water.
5. **(e)** For example perfumes and medicines.
hints: Essential oils are damaged by strong heating.

stem: Which substance is best obtained by steam distillation?

options.content: Ethanol from a fermented sugar solution
options.rationale: Ethanol is separated from water by fractional distillation.

options.content: Lemon grass oil from lemon grass leaves
options.rationale: A heat-sensitive plant oil that does not mix with water.

options.content: Pure water from sea water
options.rationale: Simple distillation is used.

options.content: Salt from sea water
options.rationale: Evaporation or crystallisation is used.

explanation: Steam distillation is used to extract volatile, heat-sensitive oils from plant material, such as lemon grass oil, eucalyptus oil or orange-peel oil.
hints: Steam distillation is for oils in plant material.

stem: True or false: in steam distillation, the plant oil distils over at a temperature below 100 °C.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: the oil comes over with the steam below 100 °C, far below its own boiling point, so it does not decompose.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: the steam carries the oil over below 100 °C. That is the whole point of the method: the oil is not overheated.

explanation: In steam distillation the oil vaporises with the steam at a temperature below 100 °C, much lower than its own boiling point, so heat-sensitive oils are not decomposed.

stem: Describe how fractional distillation separates a mixture of ethanol and water. Refer to the apparatus and explain how the fractionating column works. [6]

points.description: Heat the mixture in a flask (with anti-bumping granules), using an electric heater because ethanol is flammable
The vapour rises up a fractionating column packed with glass beads (large surface area)
The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top (temperature gradient)
Vapour repeatedly condenses and evaporates on the beads; water (higher boiling point) condenses and runs back into the flask
Ethanol (lower boiling point) reaches the top first; the thermometer at the side arm reads 78 °C
The vapour is cooled in a (water-cooled Liebig) condenser and the liquid ethanol is collected
When the temperature rises (to 100 °C), the receiver is changed and water is collected

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The mixture is heated in a round-bottomed flask with anti-bumping granules, using an electric heater because ethanol is flammable. The vapour rises into a **fractionating column** packed with glass beads, which give a large surface area. The column is **hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top**. The vapour condenses on the beads and is re-evaporated many times; **water**, with the higher boiling point (100 °C), condenses and runs back into the flask, while **ethanol**, with the lower boiling point (78 °C), reaches the top first. The thermometer at the side arm reads 78 °C. The ethanol vapour is cooled in a water-cooled condenser and collected. When the temperature rises to 100 °C, the receiver is changed and water is collected.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Award any six of the seven points.

explanation: The key ideas are the temperature gradient in the column, repeated condensation and evaporation, the lower-boiling liquid distilling first, and changing the receiver when the temperature rises.
hints: Follow the vapour from the flask, up the column, into the condenser.

stem: Which pair of miscible liquids would be **easiest** to separate by fractional distillation?

options.content: Benzene (80 °C) and cyclohexane (81 °C)
options.rationale: Boiling points only 1 °C apart are extremely hard to separate by distillation.

options.content: Ethanol (78 °C) and water (100 °C)
options.rationale: These separate, but less easily: they are only 22 °C apart.

options.content: Pentane (36 °C) and octane (126 °C)
options.rationale: The boiling points are 90 °C apart, so the liquids separate easily.

options.content: Methanol (65 °C) and propanone (56 °C)
options.rationale: These are only 9 °C apart.

explanation: The bigger the difference in boiling points, the easier the separation. Pentane and octane differ by 90 °C, by far the largest gap.
hints: Work out the difference in boiling point for each pair.

stem: Fermented sugar-cane juice contains about 10% ethanol by volume; the rest is mainly water. A student fractionally distils $500\ \text{cm}^3$ of it and collects $42\ \text{cm}^3$ of distillate at about $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$. The distillate is 95% ethanol by volume.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is fractional distillation used rather than simple distillation?

options.content: Ethanol and water are immiscible and separate into layers.
options.rationale: They mix completely.

options.content: Simple distillation only works for mixtures of two solids.
options.rationale: Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution.

options.content: They mix and boil at close temperatures, so simple distillation fails.
options.rationale: A fractionating column separates liquids with close boiling points.

options.content: Fractional distillation is faster and needs no heating at all.
options.rationale: Both methods need heating; fractional distillation gives the better separation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of ethanol in the $500\ \text{cm}^3$ of juice.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use the information about the distillate.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of ethanol in the $42\ \text{cm}^3$ of distillate.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of the ethanol in the juice that was recovered in the distillate.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why is the distillate not 100% ethanol?

options.content: The ethanol decomposes when it is heated in the flask.
options.rationale: Ethanol boils at 78 °C without decomposing.

options.content: Water from the condenser leaks into the distillate.
options.rationale: The cooling water stays in the outer jacket.

options.content: The thermometer was in the wrong place in the column.
options.rationale: The thermometer position does not change the composition of the vapour.

options.content: Some water vapour always passes over with the ethanol.
options.rationale: Even a good column gives a distillate that still contains a little water.

explanation: The juice contains $500 \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 50\ \text{cm}^3$ of ethanol. The distillate contains $42 \times \dfrac{95}{100} = 39.9\ \text{cm}^3$ of ethanol, so $\dfrac{39.9}{50} \times 100 = 79.8\%$ of the ethanol was recovered. Ethanol and water have close boiling points and mix completely, so a fractionating column is needed, and even then some water comes over with the ethanol.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** Miscible liquids with close boiling points need a fractionating column.
2. **(b)** $500 \times 0.10 = 50\ \text{cm}^3$.
3. **(c)(i)** $42 \times 0.95 = 39.9\ \text{cm}^3$.
4. **(c)(ii)** $\dfrac{39.9}{50} \times 100 = 79.8\%$ (about 80%).
5. **(d)** Some water always distils with the ethanol.
hints: 10% of 500 cm³ is the most ethanol there could be.
